security_spec.violation_condition: QEMU still emulates the MT_ASYNC bit (bit 36 in menvcfg/senvcfg/henvcfg; or the removed MT_ASYNC field in mseccfg) as a readable/writable field after the spec removed it. If QEMU's CSR emulation allows the guest to set bit 36 of *envcfg to 1, or reads back a previously-written value instead of returning 0 (WPRI), the emulation violates the updated spec. Additionally, if QEMU previously implemented deferred/asynchronous tag-check reporting for stores and that code path still exists, a guest setting the now-WPRI bit could trigger stale asynchronous behavior that the spec no longer permits.
security_spec.summary: Removal of MT_ASYNC from *envcfg bit 36 and mseccfg: if QEMU fails to convert the bit to WPRI (writes ignored, reads return 0), previously-written values leak across VM reset/context-switch boundaries, and stale asynchronous tag-check paths may create a covert side-channel observable by the guest kernel.

findings.finding: No MT_ASYNC bit (bit 36) is defined for any envcfg CSR. The menvcfg bit layout uses bits 0-7, 32-33, 59-63 with no assignment at bit 36. The only bit 36 usage in the entire cpu_bits.h is XCTRCTL_NTBREN (line 962), which is an unrelated counter-control field. No WPRI redefinition is needed because the bit was never defined in the first place.
findings.snippet:
#define MENVCFG_FIOM   BIT(0)
#define MENVCFG_LPE    BIT(2) /* zicfilp */
#define MENVCFG_SSE    BIT(3) /* zicfiss */
#define MENVCFG_PMM    (3ULL << 32)
#define MENVCFG_DTE    (1ULL << 59)
... /* bits 62-63; no bit 36 */

findings.finding: The write mask constructs the writable field set from only the defined bits (FIOM, CBIE, CBCFE, CBZE, CDE, PBMTE, STCE, ADUE, DTE, LPE, SSE, PMM). No MT_ASYNC bit exists in the mask, so any write to bit 36 is correctly masked out (write-ignored). Reserved bits default to read-as-zero, write-ignored because the mask simply doesn't include them.
senvcfg write path uses a mask of only defined fields (FIOM, CBIE, CBCFE, CBZE, PMM, LPE, SSE, UKTE). No MT_ASYNC bit. Reserved bits including bit 36 are correctly write-ignored.

henvcfg write path has a mask of defined fields plus conditional menvcfg-gated bits (PBMTE, STCE, ADUE, DTE, LPE, SSE, PMM). No MT_ASYNC bit. The code correctly ensures bits not in the mask are not writable. Reserved bits remain 0.

mseccfg write path only handles MSECCFG_MMWP (bit 1), MSECCFG_MML (bit 0), optional MSECCFG_PMM (bits 32-33), MSECCFG_RLB (bit 2), and MSECCFG_MLPE (bit 10). No MT_ASYNC field was ever defined in the mseccfg enum (pmp.h:44-50). No bit-36 field exists.
Reset values: menvcfg is initialized to PBMTE and/or ADUE based on config. henvcfg is reset to 0. No MT_ASYNC bit is set at reset. Correct per spec.
menvcfg, senvcfg, henvcfg are all included in VMState. Since no MT_ASYNC bit exists, there is no stale-field risk on migration. Migration state is correct.
findings.snippet:
VMSTATE_UINT64(env.menvcfg, RISCVCPU),
VMSTATE_UINT64(env.senvcfg, RISCVCPU),
VMSTATE_UINT64(env.henvcfg, RISCVCPU),

findings.finding: The entire trap delivery path uses 'async' only in the traditional RISC-V sense (async = interrupt, sync = exception). There is no MTE deferred-tag-check pathway, no pending-tag-mismatch buffer, and no stval2/htval2/mtval3 tag-fault write logic. The only CSR registers written during trap delivery are standard *cause, *tval, *epc, *status. No async MTE reporting pipeline exists at all.
KVM path only synchronizes senvcfg (via KVM_CSR_CFG). No MT_ASYNC bit involved. Reset sets senvcfg=0. No KVM-capable RISC-V MTE feature exists.
